title: Understanding Corporate Bonds vs. Fixed Deposits: Beyond the Interest Rate
description: Corporate bonds carry inherent credit risk, meaning the issuing company might default, unlike bank Fixed Deposits (FDs) which offer higher safety. Fixed Depos.

faq.q: Are corporate bonds always riskier than FDs?
faq.a: Yes, generally, corporate bonds carry higher credit risk than bank FDs. FDs are backed by the bank's stability and DICGC insurance up to ₹5 lakhs, whereas corporate bonds depend solely on the issuing company's financial health and ability to repay.

A credit rating is an assessment by an independent agency (like CRISIL or ICRA) of a bond issuer's ability to meet its financial obligations. It indicates the likelihood of default, with higher ratings (e.g., AAA) signifying lower risk.

faq.q: How is interest from corporate bonds taxed?
faq.a: Interest received from corporate bonds is taxable as "Income from Other Sources" and added to your total income, taxed at your applicable income tax slab rate.

faq.q: Can I lose money in a corporate bond?
faq.a: Yes, you can lose money in a corporate bond if the issuing company defaults on its payments (credit risk) or if you need to sell the bond in the secondary market before maturity at a price lower than your purchase price (market risk).

Not all. Listed corporate bonds can be traded on stock exchanges, offering liquidity. However, the actual liquidity depends on factors like the bond's credit rating, market demand, and trading volume. Less popular bonds might be difficult to sell quickly.

DICGC stands for Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, a subsidiary of the RBI. It provides deposit insurance coverage up to ₹5 lakhs for each depositor in each scheduled commercial bank in India, protecting their funds in case of bank failure.
